details:
**Jackson Pollock and the drip technique**
The best-known Abstract Expressionist, nicknamed "Jack the Dripper." He laid unstretched canvases on the floor and dripped, poured, and flung paint onto them from above. In his mature period he often titled works only with numbers. He struggled with alcoholism and died in a car crash in 1956.

**Lavender Mist and Autumn Rhythm**
Two of Pollock's most famous 1950 drip paintings. Lavender Mist (also called Number 1, 1950) is a dense web of pale, pinkish skeins of paint. Autumn Rhythm (Number 30) is a huge mural-sized canvas of black, white, and brown loops.

**Lee Krasner**
An Abstract Expressionist painter and Jackson Pollock's wife, who introduced him to the critic Clement Greenberg. Her own works include the "Little Image" series of small, dense, glyph-like marks, which has been linked to Hebrew calligraphy.

**Hans Namuth**
The photographer who, in 1950, photographed and filmed Pollock dripping paint onto canvases laid on the floor. His images made Pollock's process famous and shaped the idea of "action painting."

**Willem de Kooning's Woman series**
De Kooning was a Dutch-born leader of the movement and husband of the painter Elaine de Kooning (born Elaine Fried). His violent, gestural paintings Woman I through Woman VI, including the long-labored Woman I, partly drew on ancient Mesopotamian idols. Related works include Woman and Bicycle and his later sculpture Seated Woman on a Bench.

**Clement Greenberg and Harold Rosenberg**
The two critics who championed the movement. Greenberg wrote in the Partisan Review and promoted Pollock and later color field painting. Rosenberg coined the term "action painting" for the gestural branch of the movement, which includes Franz Kline's large black-and-white canvases such as Mahoning.

**Helen Frankenthaler's Mountains and Sea**
A 1952 painting inspired by the Nova Scotia landscape, in which Frankenthaler poured oil paint thinned with turpentine onto unprimed canvas so that it soaked in. This "soak-stain" technique was a key step toward color field painting.

**Rothko Chapel**
A nondenominational chapel in Houston, Texas, whose walls hold fourteen of Mark Rothko's dark, nearly black canvases. Rothko is the chief painter of the color field branch of Abstract Expressionism, known for soft-edged rectangles of color.

**Seagram murals**
A series of dark maroon and black murals Rothko painted for the Four Seasons restaurant in New York's Seagram Building. He said he wanted the images to ruin the appetites of the wealthy diners. He withdrew from the commission instead of finishing it, and the paintings went to museums, including the Tate in London.

**The Irascibles**
The eighteen artists who signed a 1950 open letter protesting the Metropolitan Museum of Art's exhibition "American Painting Today," which they saw as hostile to modern art. Fifteen of them posed for a famous 1951 photograph in Life magazine, in which Hedda Sterne was the only woman.

**Joan Mitchell**
A second-generation Abstract Expressionist known for energetic, landscape-inspired brushwork. Her painting Hemlock, with its green and white strokes, was inspired by Wallace Stevens's poem "Domination of Black," and her City Landscape is dominated by pinks and whites.

**Arshile Gorky's The Liver Is the Cock's Comb**
A 1944 painting by the Armenian-born Gorky, who bridged Surrealism and Abstract Expressionism and was praised by Clement Greenberg. His work was shaped by his memories of the Armenian Genocide, during which his mother died.

**Hans Hofmann and the name "Abstract Expressionism"**
Hofmann was a German-born painter whose teaching influenced many members of the movement, including Lee Krasner and Joan Mitchell. The critic Robert Coates of The New Yorker applied the term "abstract expressionism" in a 1946 review of Hofmann's work.

**Pollock's Mural for Peggy Guggenheim**
A roughly six-meter-wide 1943 canvas that the collector Peggy Guggenheim commissioned for her New York townhouse. The critic Robert Hughes called it the first painting to fully realize the goals of Abstract Expressionism.

**Full Fathom Five**
A 1947 Pollock drip painting titled after a song in Shakespeare's The Tempest. It has nails, buttons, keys, coins, and cigarette butts embedded in its thick paint.
